definition: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to that instance.
ruleOfThumb: Prefer explicit composition or dependency injection at application composition time rather than hidden globally accessible instances.

citation.author: Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides
citation.bookTitle: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the primary intent of this pattern in object-oriented designs?

options.text: Ensure only one instance of a class exists and provide a single global access point to it.
options.explanation: This pattern restricts instantiation to one object and usually exposes a single access method. It centralizes shared state and access, which is its defining intent.

options.text: Ensure a class can be easily subclassed and multiple instances coordinate shared behavior across different modules.
options.explanation: Subclassing and multiple coordinated instances describe extension and strategy concerns rather than guaranteeing a sole instance and global access point.

options.text: Provide dependency injection style decoupling so that multiple test doubles and runtime implementations are interchangeable.
options.explanation: Dependency injection emphasizes external composition and substitution, which is a different technique aimed at testability and decoupling rather than single-instance enforcement.

options.text: Encapsulate a family of algorithms behind an interface so implementations are interchangeable at runtime for callers.
options.explanation: Encapsulating interchangeable algorithms matches the Strategy pattern, not the single-instance enforcement and global access concerns of this pattern.

questions.prompt: Given this TypeScript module implementation, what is the most likely practical concern when used across an application and tests?

options.text: The module exports a shared instance, which creates hidden global state and makes replacement in tests harder.
options.explanation: Exporting a concrete instance hides the composition point and embeds global state in module boundaries. Tests cannot easily substitute or control that shared object without shimming imports.

options.text: The lazy initialization uses a nullable static and may introduce race conditions with concurrent worker threads in Node environments.
options.explanation: While worker threads or other concurrency models can expose races, Node commonly runs per-process single-threaded code. The more immediate practical problem in typical apps is the hidden global instance and testability.

options.text: The private constructor prevents subclassing and therefore disallows extension where multiple logger implementations would be useful.
options.explanation: Preventing subclassing is a real limitation, but developers often need replaceability and DI more than subclassing. The exported instance pattern primarily harms composition and testing rather than only extension.

options.text: Exporting a concrete instance tightly couples callers to a specific logger, which makes adoption of dependency injection patterns more difficult later.
options.explanation: Tight coupling to a concrete instance is a valid maintenance concern, but it is a manifestation of the hidden global state problem and not a distinct technical bug by itself.

questions.prompt: Which version is the better choice for maintainable, testable application composition when shared configuration is needed?

options.text: Version A centralizes a single exported instance which simplifies access but hides state and prevents easy test replacement.
options.explanation: Version A provides convenience but couples consumers to a hidden module-level instance. That coupling obstructs test isolation and makes different runtime compositions or per-request variations awkward to implement.

options.text: Version B favors explicit construction and composition time wiring which makes substitution and testing straightforward.
options.explanation: Version B externalizes the creation point so the application composes the desired instance. This enables different environments or test doubles to be injected without touching module internals, improving testability and architecture. References: Martin Fowler on dependency injection and composition; GoF discussion on object creational patterns and their tradeoffs.
